utterances.text: Okay. Let me repeat the question so to make sure that we have a correct answer from you. Obviously, your commander trusted you to go and pass along, convey his order to the guards. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he trusted me; I think he did but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he asked you to go there, did he not?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was sometime after he had given the order to Nikolic to make sure that the prisoners were not mistreated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes. That was when we went home, on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. So it wasn't that he just told Nikolic and rested back and figured that Nikolic, given his propensity for kindness to his fellow human beings would do the right and honourable thing, he wanted you as well to go there and to convey his direct and specific orders to the guards that were guarding the prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say -- could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Momir Nikolic was head of security, was he not?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police are under his supervision, are they not?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The military police, according to you, were guarding the prisoners there, were they not?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Colonel Blagojevic doesn't say, "Momir," or "Little Pensioner," which is his little nickname, as I understand, or "Nedjo," how he likes to call himself, whatever, he doesn't say, "Go there and check up." Rather, he asks you after he tells Nikolic to make sure that he doesn't do anything stupid.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He told me to go on my way home, just to drop by on my way home. This was all in passing and just to tell him if there's something wrong. But everything was all right, just to continue on home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Logically speaking though, sir, would that not have been Nikolic's job for the colonel to say to Nikolic, "Go check up on the men and come back and report to me if there's something wrong." Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He probably told him also. He said something there, but I didn't hear what he told him later and I didn't know what Nikolic said either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But assuming that he did tell Nikolic, he's telling you just to be on the safe side or in addition to. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm objecting to that. That's obviously speculative and we're coming to a point where --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've made my point, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: -- it's becoming an argument, As opposed to question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm driving the nail all the way through to the other end on this matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next day, that would make it the 13th of July, 1995, and on that particular day I take it you don't have a vivid recollection what, if anything, you did with the commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember one day, that day when we went to the logistics base and we came back quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the logistics base would have, as you indicated, they would have the supplies like - I wrote it down here - bread and foodstuff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if prisoners needed to be fed, or if food needed to go to the folks that were in Potocari, I guess that's where they would come from. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't know where that would come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless, those sorts of supplies are located there?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the 13th we heard testimony here that it was believed that on that particular day Colonel Blagojevic's mother was ill and that a doctor was taken to visit her at the village. Do you know whether your commander went there to visit his mother?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it possible, sir, given your previous testimony, that the colonel did not -- you did not always travel with the colonel, with the commander, that he could have gone to visit his mother without taking you along, specifically given the nature of the visit?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He would go and visit his mother by himself, too, or maybe this Goran who was with me also went, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on one day, it's unclear exactly which particular date it is, because as you've indicated you're having some problems with the dates, but on one day you indicated that you saw Colonel Blagojevic and he looked extremely concerned.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes, probably, because of his mother, because his mother was not feeling very well over those few days, that's what I've heard, and so he was worried about his mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But he didn't express to you the reasons?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not ask him or anyone else. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I didn't ask him. I don't know if anybody else did, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point you indicated that you went with the commander towards the Milici Brigade or to the headquarters of the Milici Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know the nature of that particular visit?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's unclear to you how many days after the fall of Srebrenica you had actually gone there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And it was -- was it during that trip on the way back that you stopped at Konjevic Polje or in that vicinity where the commander saw his troops and talked to them?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they on the road or were they off the road? Were they searching the terrain? Because we know that there were orders to search the terrain as of the 14th. Do you know what exactly they might have been doing there?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: They were on the road, but I don't know what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, as I understand your -- as I understand your testimony, once again it was your impression that your commander was giving instructions that nothing was supposed to -- that they were not supposed to mistreat any prisoners if they came across any. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That they were supposed to act professionally. Correct? I believe that was the word that you used.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: That they should behave properly and fair, and that they should bring them to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I wanted to get to. And also he had instructed them that if they came across anybody, anyone, that they were to come all the way to the brigade as opposed to some other holding place, some other detention place, but to come all the way there to the brigade headquarters where he was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be, sir, that he was asking them or instructing them to bring them all the way to the brigade headquarters so he could ensure that nothing happened to these prisoners that were captured by his particular men, versus what might have been going on by others?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Probably to be sure that they are brought there alive and well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. And after you left on the road you came across someone who was injured. Right?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that he was dressed in fatigues, in army fatigues.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He had a military top, a shirt, and military -- army boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it from looking at the way he was dressed, you could not tell whether he was a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether he had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, meaning that he did not have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He didn't have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you speak to this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I asked him whether he had any documents, and the colonel came out and he asked him, too, but he just kept quiet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "he kept quiet," in other words he did not produce any documents to show that he was a Serb soldier in the vicinity carrying on some activities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He didn't show us anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, given the circumstances, did that not strike you as somewhat odd, if he had been a Serb soldier? Why would he not show his documents to another Serb officer?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Probably he didn't have them on him. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be that he was a Muslim who was in the area and not a Serb?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was a Muslim or a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the commander ask this person, who looked like he needed help who was injured? Did you hear your commander ask whether he was a Serb or a Muslim, so he perhaps could make a decision how to treat this particular individual?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Well, I think the commander heard me ask him for his documents, but he was just silent. He didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- but in other words the commander never made a request as to whether that particular individual who was injured and needed help and had no documents, in that particular time, under those circumstances, at that location, whether he was a Serb or a Muslim? He didn't ask him what his background was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No. At that point the truck turned up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And he instructed or he requested the truck to take this unknown individual, be he a Muslim who was trying to make his way to Srebrenica or be he a Serb soldier who was there, to take that individual to the hospital so that individual could get some help. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you took another trip with the colonel, and before we get to that one I wanted to discuss a little bit the document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday when you were here meeting with them in their office when they were getting you ready for your testimony here today. Okay. And the document that I'm referring to was previously admitted, for the record, as P496. If you could look at -- I have P96B [sic] which is the Srpski version of it, or B/C/S as it is referred to in this court or this Tribunal. If you could look at that, sir, is that the document that was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on that particular day, July 16th, just to give you a basis of what they were talking about, it's the day before Colonel Blagojevic goes off to Zepa. All right. At least that's the testimony that we have from this courtroom, that on the 17th of July the colonel himself went off to Zepa at some point. All right. Now, I don't know if that's going to help you. But let me ask this question, because I was a little unclear and maybe you can help us out here: As far as I understand, having searched your memory, you do not recall the commander visiting any of these troops or locations on July 16th, as this daily report reflects?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, would you have remembered visiting these locations, assuming that this trip actually had occurred, as opposed to merely putting something on writing and handing it over to the Drina Corps, for the purposes of showing that a task that was given was actually performed?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you were on duty on that particular day - and I haven't heard that you weren't - and if you don't recall visiting any of these sites with the commander where he might have been giving all of these instructions, could it be, sir, that the reason that you don't remember is because this never occurred? In other words, the commander never visited all these places even though we have this piece of document stating that he had performed those tasks?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't remember that, so it's not something that I know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you do know these places that are reflected in this document? I mean --

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall ever going to these places and maybe not recalling the date? And it's okay if you don't.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I guess you can't remember a place if you've never been to it. Okay. Now, we know that the commander goes off with his troops on the 17th of July. That seems to be what I would call a fact beyond change. We know it. And we heard you tell us that at one point in time you drove some 600 to 700 kilometres with the commander when he went off to visit, inspect, check up on, look after, his troops in Drvar. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is -- and incidentally, on that particular trip you stayed there for two or three days. Right?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given the distance, it would seem to me that it would take several hours to get there.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, to go from Bratunac all the way there, to Drvar, if it's between 6 and 700 kilometres, it would take several hours to go there by car.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, do you recall whether this was before or after the commander went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as you recall, this trip occurred after the trip when you went to the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it possible, sir, that this trip to Drvar could have taken place sometime between -- sometime before he went off to Zepa, before the 17th of July, and maybe you didn't stay two or three days, maybe you just stayed one day or just two days? Is that possible? I don't know. I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that either, when that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you can't tell us yes or no? It could be -- could be that it happened before the 17th, it could be that it happened after the 17th. You just cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nonetheless, just so we have it right, so the Honourable Members of our Trial Chamber know exactly what's over there, there were battalions from the Bratunac Brigade in Drvar. Correct? There were soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade there. Right?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the things the commander did when he was there is check up and see how his men are doing, like a good commander should be doing under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I have a few more questions, but not that many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you by any chance go to Zepa with the commander, or did you stay behind at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember what happened to the lines, where the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th Battalions were located, or whether the lines shifted, or moved or disappeared after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know when the commander came back from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It sounds to me, sir, from your testimony that Colonel Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, during that period of time was trying to make sure that all of his men acted properly towards everyone. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you being close to him, being with him, travelling with him, you never saw him act in any way or encourage anyone or instruct anyone to commit any crimes against anyone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very, very, much, sir, I appreciate your testimony and I'm sure it will be extremely helpful to the members of this Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for this witness, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, just a couple of questions. Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Issa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any knowledge of anyone being killed after the fall of Srebrenica, any Muslims being many killed after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the Vuk Karadzic school, sir, did you see members of the Red Cross at that school or in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe, Your Honour, we had any testimony, unless I'm mistaken, that on the 12th, the evening of the 12th that there was anybody from the Red Cross there. Now, I could be wrong, but I certainly don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, I think your re-direct should be closely related to the questions asked by Mr. Karnavas in the cross-examination. I could not remember him asking any questions about the Red Cross presence at that time, unless you could show us there is some connections with the questions asked in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there were a number of questions relating to the Vuk Karadzic school and what he had seen and suggestions put to the witness. And it would be my submission that this might be a relevant fact in relation -- given these suggestions that Mr. Karnavas put to the witness in relation to the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this question should be asked in direct examination rather than the re-direct. I hope your question could be asked closely related to the questions put by Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas, do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nothing further, based on that excellent, excellent ruling, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honour, I do have a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked -- it was put to you in cross-examination that you had the opportunity to look around to see -- when you were at the Vuk Karadzic school to see whether atrocities were occurring. Did you go inside the gym? Did you see any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I didn't go inside the gym, but I heard stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you "heard stories" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe that there might have been a mistranslation, Your Honour. If the question can be asked again. I don't want to suggest what the gentleman indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let's clarify this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, the question was: Did you go inside the gym? Did you see any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated, sir, that you went to the logistics base where you were -- saw bread and food. Can you indicate how much bread and food you saw there.

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I didn't see either bread or food, just food was stored at the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how do you know that food was stored there?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Well, I know. I went into the logistics base previously, not then, but I know that they had food, clothing, blankets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just by way of clarification, sir, you were asked some questions in relation to the day that Srebrenica fell when you went back to the Bratunac Brigade. You were asked -- you said that in your cross-examination that you were not sure if you had seen Colonel Blagojevic around 6.00 -- 5.00 or 6.00, but you did see him late in the afternoon. My question is if you can clarify that. Was that in the afternoon, as well as in the evening when you saw him leave? Or when was that? How many times did you see him that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Compound question. Let the witness answer. Let's not try to encourage him with multiple choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I believe those questions are related questions, and we'll see how the witness will answer this question. If the witness cannot understand it, I believe, Ms. Issa, you have to break up the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to clarify it by that last question, Your Honour. Perhaps I can just put it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see the colonel that day when you returned to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: When I returned, the colonel was already at the brigade. So that was sometime late in the afternoon. I apologise if I got the time wrong, but I can't tell you exactly. But that's roughly when it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see him another time after that sighting that you had of him at the brigade that same day?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: He was at the brigade until the evening, until he left to go to his apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have one matter. It does not relate to this issue, but it's a point of clarification because I think the Prosecution is trying to paint the man as being dishonest by saying that --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to object to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The comments that Mr. Karnavas is making are totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do not make this kind of statement in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question relates to whether he was aware of any killings. The question should be asked did he hear of any killings. Because I think there's a linguistic nuance here that leaves the impression that somehow he's trying to hide evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've gotten used to the accusations, but not in front of a witness that's trying to answer the questions, that has yet to answer the Judge's questions. This witness has done a lot to come up here out of his schedule and for him to make up this thing that -- to make it personal, it's outrageous, it's outrageous. And I wish you could please instruct him to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely suggesting the way -- because of the linguistic difference, it gives the appearance that the witness, being over there, never heard of anything, obviously then it negates a great deal of his testimony. And I think that linguistic difference needs to be cleared up. So I would appreciate to ask the witness whether he heard, because I think when you say "aware," to them would be the understanding whether they saw --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, if Mr. Karnavas is going to go on, I'm going to ask that the witness be removed from the room, because this is totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you had the opportunity to cross-examine this witness already. And since you mentioned that it is a linguistic issue, I believe that the Trial Chamber will look into it, or if necessary will ask for the assistance of the interpretation booth on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I would like to have the witness posed the question because there is a distinction between being aware in the sense of seeing, versus hearing of it. And if a witness says: "I wasn't aware of anything," it gives the impression that the witness may be being -- being untruthful in that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any questions from the Judges? Judge Vassylenko? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Gospodine Svedok, have you testified before this Tribunal before?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And when for the first time you were interviewed by the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: Six days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And then my last question: Were you aware about the killings, or you have heard about the killings?

utterances.speaker: How do you know or anything -- something to that effect.  But
utterances.text: I didn't hear about any killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions. Hvala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges questions? Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are a couple of documents. P680, which was the map; P681, the aerial marked by the witness; P720, the sketch; P721, the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections? Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I would ask that they all be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, those documents are admitted into the evidence under seal. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your testimony. I understand you overcame a lot of difficulties to travel here. We appreciate it very much. The usher will show you out of the room when she pulls down the blinds. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, are we going to hear the next witness this afternoon, or you prefer we hear it tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- the latest I've heard was that there is bad fog in Zagreb and the witness was on the Tarmac. And as you probably know this time of year that can be a problem. So far between everyone's work and all and weather, we've been very lucky. And We appreciate very much everyone, including the Defence's, efforts to put on this witness this week. It looks like the weather might be against us. Oh, I might have some update. Today obviously not, we're hoping tomorrow. And I hope that my direct will only be one session. That is the way I have -- the flight's left Zagreb, so it looks good for tomorrow. And unfortunately, I guess there's no courtroom in the morning, but we will be able to proceed in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have been told by the registrar that we have secured a courtroom tomorrow afternoon, that is Courtroom III. We'll start at 2.15. Since we still have a session, I don't think we should waste that time. So we may spend some time on the procedural matters, including the 92 bis documents. So we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we still have some time, we'll deal with the admission of the documents in accordance with the rule, 92 bis. I think the other day this Bench instructed the registrar to work with the Prosecution concerning of certain documents which proposed by the Prosecution to tender through 92 bis. This is an oral decision in relation to the admission of those documents. The Trial Chamber has reviewed the list presented by the Prosecution in relation to the admission of the exhibits related to these witnesses. Upon careful study of the list, the Trial Chamber found it is appropriate under 92 bis to admit the documents submitted through those witnesses. The set of documents in question are: Exhibits P780, P788, 789, 781, 790, 791, 782, 792, 793, 794, 795, 796, 797, 798, 799, 800, 783, 784, 801, 802, 803, 785, 786, 804, and P787. It is so decided. The other set of documents is that the Prosecution has filed a motion for the admission of documents on the 23rd of February. The motion requests admission of three sets of documents. The first set, 209 documents listed in the footnotes of the expert report of Mr. Butler, which were not tendered by either party during his examination. The second set of documents are 14 documents of the ABiH 28th Infantry Division, dated 13th June to 10th July, 1995. The third set of documents is a MUP report from Zvornik security centre dated 12th July, 1995. This Trial Chamber understands that there are no problems of disclosure or authentication with respect to these documents. It also notes that according to the motion the Defence has not objected to their admission. At this moment we would like to reiterate the principle for the admission of the documents. Under Rule 89(C), the Trial Chamber may admit any relevant evidence it deems to have probative value. This rule leaves a lot of discretion to the Trial Chamber in its decision to admit evidence or not. This rule should, however, be interpreted in light of the Trial Chamber's duty to ensure a fair and expeditious trial under Article 20 and 21 of the Statute. In this respect, the Trial Chamber's ability to assess the relevance and the reliability of the evidence presented varies as the case developed. The Trial Chamber are in the position to exercise more control over the evidence to be presented at the end of the Prosecution's case than it is at the beginning of the trial. One particular way of ensuring an expeditious trial is to exclude evidence that is repetitious. As a result, the documents represented at this stage of trial should not be of purely cumulative nature. It should not be a pure repetition of the evidence already admitted, but should add details and information which contributes to a better understanding or assessment of the evidence presented. Furthermore, evidence should, as a rule, be presented in court in order to respect the rights of the accused to a public trial and have the evidence tested in court, especially through the cross-examination. Admission from the bar table should be an exception and could mainly concern official documents which cannot be contested, such as UN reports, resolutions, et cetera. To be more specific, we will deal with the first set of 209 documents linked to Butler's testimony. First, the Trial Chamber's decision dated on 7th November, 2003, only admitted Mr. Butler's report. It did not intend to implicitly admit all documents referred to in the footnotes of the report. As a rule, sources and references on the basis of which the expert reaches his or her conclusions should be clearly mentioned in the report, and such is the purpose of the footnotes. The sources mentioned therein should also be disclosed to the other party if requested. There is, however, no obligation for the parties to tender all the documents referred to in the report as exhibits. To the contrary, both parties have the discretion to tender whatever document they deem would best serve their case. A number of the documents were indeed tendered and admitted this way during the examination of Mr. Butler. At this stage, the parties chose not to tender those 209 documents admitted through the motion. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber cannot admit the 209 documents, as it has not seen, on the mere basis that the Defence does not object. The Prosecution would need to indicate why those documents would be necessary at this stage of the trial, in view of the principle reminded above. As it stands, the motion is not sufficiently substantiated in respect of those documents. It is therefore rejected. It is so decided. As for the second set of documents, that is, the 14 documents of the ABiH 28th Division, the documents are not submitted and the Chamber does not know what they are about exactly. In view of the arguments represented by the Prosecution, a few questions arise; however, first, these documents are dated between the 30th of June and the 10th of July, 1995, according to the indictment. The counts charge acts which occurred between 12th and the 19th of July. As a result, these documents seem to refer to background information rather than specific counts of the indictment. Secondly, in particular could the Prosecution explain to what extent the three elements it raises in its motion refer to the specific counts in the indictment, namely targeting the shelling of civilian targets in the Srebrenica enclave, the rising intensity and the temper of attack on Srebrenica when the attack on Srebrenica began, the conditions of life present in the enclave shortly after and during the time period relevant to the indictment. In addition, is this point purely corroborating evidence or does it add to the evidence already adduced? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. These few 28th Division documents -- one is a little bit different than the rest. The one that's dated 30 June isn't -- is a clear -- it's a document where the 28th Division clearly indicates there was a policy at the highest levels of their army to create havoc outside the enclave in order to draw VRS troops from the Sarajevo area. This was a background piece of information, something that Mr. Butler, I believe, touched on. I know it was something the Defence was interested in. It was never clearly stated so in black and white, as it is in that one document. And we just thought that you would be interested in that particular clear concise viewpoint of the BiH's attitude at that point. While we look at that as background and not particularly relevant to the crimes that later occur, we have always stressed and tried to stress in this case that Srebrenica did not occur in a vacuum, and that we tried to show the perspective of the 28th Division as well as, of course, the VRS. So that was just such a clear statement of their policy, which I know Mr. Karnavas had spent some time on in cross-examination, that we thought -- and I can tell you it was a document from the past case that the Court took some interest in. I know Courts are different, of course, but we thought of that and thought that that as well as the collection that I'll get to would have been something important for you just to see, because it was such a clear statement. If there were any questions about the 28th Division and what they were doing, this document helps point that out. One of the reasons I point to the prior case is that in this case, as you know, we did not call any Bosnian generals, Halilovic or Hadzihasanovic, who are both on trial here. This piece of the evidence went to what the last Court was interested in, and that's why they called those folks. So we just thought, in our housekeeping and in looking through the material, I thought this is something important that you should see and may want to see. So that's that one document. The other documents go to the count of forcible transfer, the -- and I know you're very familiar with the historical lead-up of the various Karadzic documents that say make life unbearable in the enclave, the document that says restrict the convoys, and Mr. Butler's interpretation that the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, reducing the enclave to its urban area was to help create a humanitarian disaster. So one of the main points of these, what are basically combat reports that you're very familiar with and the VRS perspective, were to show that the situation, the humanitarian situation was becoming more dire as the days went on. And this is a particularly important point regarding Mr. Blagojevic. As you may remember, the July -- there's a report signed in the early weeks of July that is the half-year report on the situation in the Bratunac Brigade, where there is mention of their responsibility regarding convoys. And this -- these 28th Division reports show that the convoys are not coming in at that time and people, as a result, are starving. It's the view of the Prosecution that this is precisely the intent of the -- President Karadzic, General Mladic, and the VRS, including the Bratunac Brigade, as indicated in Mr. Ognjenovic's report, you may remember that from 1994 that actually states that policy, and as adopted or taken over by Mr. Blagojevic. So the simple direct statements of things are getting worse and worse, we're not getting food from the convoys goes to the issue of squeezing the enclaves in creating a situation where the Muslim population would have to leave. So that's forcible transfer, right on point, some of the most clear evidence we have on that point. I think Muslims have testified about how it was difficult, but this was a more official viewpoint of that. The other point that this material talks about is the shelling of the town, of the hospital for example. This evidence, as it has come in through General Kingori and the UN military observers is very important for the forcible transfer case because it shows that there was a pattern of shelling of civilian targets, both during the attack and even after the 11th there were some -- still some shelling. And when you -- if you look at the UN military observer reports of each day of shelling the town, then now you have the 28th Division reports to look at which also talks about shelling the town on the same day. So as opposed to relying on one set of documents from the UN, we have 28th Division documents that help support that shelling actually did occur. And we also, you'll see, from the daily combat reports of the Bratunac Brigade that they're using quite a bit of artillery shells each day during this case and there is evidence that the Drina Corps in the attack, including the troops involved, were in fact shelling civilian targets, which of course goes to the -- again, the forcible transfer, the intent of the army and the commanders in it to scare these people out of the enclave. So those 28th Division documents give us a very clear and unambiguous statement of the shelling and a very clear and unambiguous statement of the conditions as they worsened as a result of not getting materials from the convoys. So while there is evidence on both these areas, this, I think, is additional reliable and corroborative -- I would like to say corroborative as opposed to cumulative evidence. So we ask that you view it. I felt that the combat reports themselves were very clear, unambiguous. They certainly didn't need any expert to talk about what they were. We all recognise that they are coming from the 28th Division, and as such they certainly have reasons of their own and may have some bias to them, like any army may have a bias. And I don't think that is in question. That's why I ask you to look at them in comparison to the other evidence, the UNMO evidence, the evidence related to the Dutch observations. So that's what I would say about the -- those combat reports of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have some -- I have a response. It would appear that now the indictment is expanded and now, without stating it in the indictment, now Mr. Blagojevic is now also being charged for the attack on Srebrenica, if we follow that line of thinking. I'm sure that Mr. McCloskey is not thinking in those terms, but I think that one from this aisle listening to that explanation walks away with that conclusion. Why do I say that? I do agree with him with the one document, because I tried from day one and was curtailed, perhaps because the Trial Chamber was not aware of my strategy and my theory of the case, into going into Naser Oric and the 28th Division, into the killings and lootings of the Serb population that was being done with impunity under the eyes, and perhaps even with the assistance of the UN DutchBats who were there supposedly to demilitarise the area, but were giving sanctuary to those criminals who were out there committing those crimes. Secondly, we did present some evidence through Mr. Butler with respect to the situation on the ground. As the war was progressing, it was clear, it was clear as night follows day, that at some point the Muslim army was getting ready for an assault on the Serbs. We -- and one need only look at the Milosevic case where there's testimony come in. We will be asking Carl Bildt to come here and testify because he gives a pretty good explanation that during the negotiating process while these things are going on, the Muslims are being -- are growing in numbers, the arms are being shipped in from the United States, the weapons are being shipped in from the United States and others. In fact, Carl Bildt even indicates that Karadzic was even excluded and they were only negotiating with Mladic at the time, so they could put a wedge between Karadzic and Mladic. But there's documentation that at some point in a near distant future the Serbs were going to be facing an assault, an offensive, by the Muslim forces. And we know already that Tudjman and his army was also being helped by the Americans and provided with weapons. So I think this does give context, which is one of the reasons why when I had Mr. Butler on the stand he admitted that militarily speaking the attack on Srebrenica was -- made sense at that particular time because it was much better for the VRS to be on the offensive as opposed to being on the defensive later on. So that was what was playing out on the ground. And I agree with Mr. McCloskey that there was testimony with respect to that. Be that as it may, I would have liked for us to have had this discussion here with those particular documents, because then it allows me the opportunity to do cross-examination, which is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Statute. With respect to the rest, and this is where I believe there seems to be an attempt and probably, you know, just as a result of trying to get the documents in, but I think there's an attempt to expand the scope of the indictment. Obviously, contextually, I think these documents might be relevant if they were brought in through witnesses and we could have some sort of a dialogue, some sort of evidence, with respect to these documents so you could understand the documents in perspective. These documents -- the Prosecution had ample opportunity to bring in Muslim witnesses. They have AID, which I understand is a secret service of the Bosniaks assisting the Office of the Prosecution, they could have had those folks come in. Whether the generals would like to come in and assist the Prosecutor this time as they did in Krstic, probably not, less cooperative at this point now that they are indicted, accused, and are in the middle of a trial of their own --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We should be clear that they were brought in by the Court during the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By the Court, I apologise. Nonetheless, at the time they were brought in by the Court, they were not aware that they either had been indicted or were in the process of being indicted. So perhaps now that they're here they are less happy to be cooperative, either with the Court, the Prosecution, or the Defence. But I think all of these documents, what the Prosecution is trying to establish is that there is sort of a plan, and it all fits in nicely and neatly into their theory that this was a genocide that actually was preplanned, not days or months, but perhaps even years prior to the fall of Srebrenica. Although, if we take that and we juxtapose it as to what we heard from Mr. McCloskey as to what the 28th Division was doing and the strategy which was pin down the VRS troops, it would seem there was something else in play. In addition to that, there's also, as we understand it - there's documentation and I'm sure the Prosecution knows better than I - that the government of BiH, the Sarajevo government, the Muslim government at the time, was preventing the Muslims from leaving Srebrenica because that was their political chip and it enabled them to tie down the VRS. And so they were using them for that purposes -- for those purposes. And of course at the same time there are these negotiations and Carl Bildt, if we are lucky enough to get him here, will testify that there was some sort of dialogue at the time as to giving greater land around Sarajevo to the Muslims, and Srebrenica be given to the RS. In other words, no ethnic cleansing, instead exchange of territories. This is another political gamesmanship that's going on between other players at a different level, before and perhaps even during these events. And so the question is: If we're going to allow this kind of stuff to come in, will I be able as part of my case to go into these documents and to go into this and to bring witnesses? Because now what we're trying -- what the Prosecution is doing, as I've indicated, is expanding the scope. And they would have us believe, at least from where I'm sitting, that the attack on Srebrenica was a crime, and it's not charged as a crime in the indictment. And when you get to what I just heard, that, you know, the poor people there were starving, well, I agree. The humanitarian aid was being cut off, but as you recall, Your Honour, early on, when I had Mr. Ruez -- and perhaps in the Court's mind at the time there was a misunderstanding or a suspicion that I was trying to justify what had happened because of what Naser Oric was doing. I believe there is a particular principle, tu quoque, which obviously, as I indicated to the Court, that wasn't my -- I was aware of the principle and that wasn't my point. But what I was trying to get out and what I would like to get out then -- now, if this evidence comes in, that in Srebrenica, in fact there were a lot of supplies, but Naser Oric, being the war criminal and war profiteer that he was, was storing all of those food supplies while he was acting as a little warlord over there in Srebrenica. The question why he wasn't there when Srebrenica fell, that's an interesting issue. There are lots of different theories. Some may be that if he's not there the 28th Division will leave as opposed to sit there and fight. The question has always been: Why didn't the 28th Division at least try to take the weapons away from the Dutch and make some sort of fight against the VRS forces. And if that had happened I think history would have been written slightly differently. So what am I getting at? What I'm getting at all of this is the following: This was not part of the Prosecution's case as they presented it. I do agree to some extent with Mr. McCloskey that this is information that might be relevant and important to the Trial Chamber. But if they want this information to come in, at this stage while they still are on their case in-chief, they should present that evidence, as opposed to back-dooring it, by just saying, here, here's some evidence, here's some documents, read it, factor it in. I think it puts us at a disadvantage. It certainly -- as I said, it seems to expand the indictment. And now I'm forced to fight on a different front as well. Lastly, I would -- how should I put it? I would welcome the opportunity to have those witnesses come in so we could discuss these documents, because we do believe that if we put them into perspective that the Trial Chamber will have a fuller view in deciding what exactly happened before, during, and after. But I think at this stage, I don't know whether this was a tactical decision, or if this was an error on their part or a -- something that they overlooked. It's a huge case, and so it's not unusual to overlook, you know, parts of the strategy of the case. It could also be that they were challenged, challenged in the sense that they couldn't bring in the witnesses to make the foundation to get the documents in. I don't know. But I think at this stage it's a little too late in the game to bring them in this way. But I don't object, I don't object, if the Prosecutor wishes to put on additional witnesses and prolong their case, because they haven't rested yet and I want to give them the fullest and fairest opportunity to put on as long and as big of a case as they possibly can, because at the end of the day I think this Trial Chamber will have to conclude that Vidoje Blagojevic is not guilty of anything that he is charged with in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall try briefly to explain the reasons for which we, after talking to Mr. McCloskey, said that we are not against having this -- these exhibits tendered. And after the discussions today, the question remains open as to what the substance is of having all these exhibits tendered and introduced. And I'd like to focus my -- what I have to say on the reports of the command of the 28th Division of the BH army. I'm talking about those exhibits, and the first reason that guided us not to object to having this exhibit admitted into evidence is the report which is called: "Regular combat report -- daily combat report of the 30th of June," where the 28th Division, that is to say one of the units from the Srebrenica enclave undoubtedly sports the thesis of the Defence that the safe area of Srebrenica, under one, was not demilitarised, and under two, that they had active combat operations pursuant to orders from the BH army and the command of the Main Staff of the BH army, precisely in order, as they say here, to disburden the Sarajevo area region. And thus launched offensive operations that they set out here and thus let it be known that they do have the potential and the ability to carry something like that out. The quotations and allegations from the Krivaja 95 combat order say that those were the reasons for which that operation was undertaken. The second argument that we use in saying this was that the daily combat report of the 28th Division of the BH Army dated the 6th of July in which, on page 2, it says that: "After an offensive operation was carried out, there was a conflict between" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's too fast. Slow down. We have plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, I was talking about the daily combat report, dated the 6th of July, in which it clearly states that a conflict had taken place between the members of the 28th Division and the Army of Republika Srpska, and that on that occasion the BH Army, or rather, the 28th Division repelled all attacks launched by the Army of Republika Srpska. This also -- is also confirmed by a series of daily combat reports from the Zvornik Brigade about the very heavy and difficult fighting that took place in the Srebrenica area and the fact that on that occasion there were substantial losses in the Army of Republika Srpska. The third document that I should like to mention and which we consider to be relevant is the daily combat report of the 8th of July, 1995, in which on page 2 we see mention of the fact that in the area of the Srebrenica safe area there was a total of 60.000 Muslims, or rather, Bosniaks. Now, this figure can be of importance, both for the expert testimony of Mr. Helge Brunborg and the existence of genocide. Bearing in mind the information about the number of inhabitants that this honourable Tribunal had before it thus far, it can be relevant, in our opinion. And finally, we have the last report dated the 5th of July in which we can see that in the safe area of the enclaves, the Srebrenica enclave as a safe area, that the humanitarian convoy of the UNHCR did arrive and it was on the basis of that convoy that flour was distributed and the other supplies that were necessary. So this fact, too, indicates what the Defence presented during the case, and that is that at the time of combat operations on both sides, the flow of humanitarian aid and assistance was always present. Now, whether it was sufficient, whether there was sufficient humanitarian aid or not, that is an open question with respect to the capabilities of the UNHCR and UNPROFOR, and not whether it was a systematic and planned political decision to prevent and ban the entry of the convoy carrying humanitarian aid into the safe area. So it is precisely for those reasons that we assume the positions we did in order to demonstrate the thesis that the Defence always held through the testimony and examination of Mr. Ruez and also Mr. Mandzic, and through examining Mr. Mandzic and we tried to prove that through questioning them and their testimony. I think that Your Honours, you yourselves have seen that those daily combat reports are dated from the 30th of June until the 10th of July, and therefore outside the time span and that we have no report during intensive fighting and the breakthrough of the column itself of the members of the 28th Division, that is to say from the 11th up until the 16th of July and to all intents and purposes, until they arrived on the territory under the control of the BH Army and that is the relevant period for my client as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll give a few minutes to Mr. McCloskey for the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just as Mr. Stojanovic's words are in our memory, I think that he found some of the details historically helpful to sort out those early -- those key days, and fundamentally that's an important reason. You may find it helpful. We are obviously relying on the combat reports of the VRS. We should look at the combat reports of the 28th Division as well. In those reports -- the author of most of them Ramiz Becirovic, who was the acting commander in the absence of Naser Oric, died of, I believe, a heart attack after the war. His commanders, as we've mentioned, two of them are currently on trial. And of course, I could have brought forward any Bosnian army person or person in the enclave and asked them about these documents. However, at some point, as Your Honour is aware, I have made a huge effort to pick each witness individually and not add anything that might be extra. And at some point a document is so basic that it really doesn't -- we don't need -- it's like what they say about experts. We loan them our watch to tell us what time it is. We don't need an expert to tell us what our watch says. These things have five or ten points in them, which I think are all potentially of historical interest. A witness would have been cumulative, time-consuming and I don't think anyone really contests this in any significant way. Mr. Karnavas agreed to allow this material in, is my understanding with Mr. Waespi. He has every chance to change his mind. It throws me off a little bit because when Mr. Karnavas and I agree on something, it's cause for celebration and we don't normally get as perhaps tough as we might in a motion. And so we just tried to lay it out. And I can tell you, this is not trying to broaden the indictment. This is evidence of the forcible transfer, just like we listed a lot of the evidence in the indictment, the various documents that show there was an intent to move these people out. This is just evidence. This is not expanding it in any way. This is just evidence that they wanted to scare them out of town. And this is not some plan to suggest or to argue that this -- there is a pre-planned genocide in place. This is for another trial. I'm not concentrating on whether there was a pre-planned genocide or not; it's for another trial. It's hard for me to imagine -- beginning a serious plan of killing people until you know you have people to kill. So that's why I focused you on the night of the 11th of July when the VRS first realises that they have an a significant number of Muslim men. What happened before that in terms of genocidal plans is in Belgrade and for another case which is not something I'm trying to take you down that road to. I would like to keep us on point in this case, ideally from July 1 up until about September, October 1995. I also -- Mr. Butler chooses his own documents. I don't tell Mr. Butler what documents to pick. He picked a few reports around these dates - I don't recall exactly what they were - for particular things he wanted to say. I can always ask Mr. Butler and sometimes I have to say "Mr. Butler, can you put in your report a section on something or other so the Judges will know that." I generally don't do that often, and this is a particular case where I didn't. This doesn't mean that these eight, nine, ten reports aren't something that are important and I think they speak for themselves. And of course you're the best Judges after, like you say, hearing all the -- just about all the Prosecution's case whether you think they're important or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after hearing the parties and after consultations with my colleague, we believe that those documents that are dated between 30th of June and the 10th of July, 1995, they did not go to the actual conduct and acts by both accused, they are just background information documents. And some of them are corroborating the evidence presented in this courtroom. So it's entirely within the scope of the 92 bis scope, and we found that those documents have some probative value in themselves. At the same time, I would like to remind the parties, this is a trial with two accused, namely Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic. The attack on Srebrenica, the military manoeuvre of both sides are not the subject matter of this case. The purpose of this trial is to understand whether the two accused are guilty or not. It is our duty to stop any attempts, if there's any, to expand the scope of the indictment at this stage, especially for the nature of the armed conflict, that is to say whether a military manoeuvre is justified or not, unless those military manoeuvres are closely related to the charges listed in the indictment. At the same time, we also found that those documents, if admitted, will also help the Defence to prepare their case in the future. In past proceedings we received very few so-called official documents of the ABiH. So based on the above reasons, we decided to admit those 14 documents into evidence without cross-examination. It is so decided. I hope Mr. Court Deputy will contact the Prosecution to give them proper numbers for those documents. The last set of documents are the MUP reports from Zvornik security centre dated 12 July 1995. The question we would like to ask to the Prosecution is: To what extent does it add to the evidence already adduced? We hope the Prosecution could be more specific on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. To fully answer that, I would best need the two or three other very similar reports drafted -- done by the same person, Dragomir Vasic, the head of the Zvornik municipality CSB. He writes a series of reports on this critical day of 12 July. He writes, as you recall, there's one that says he is at an 8.30 a.m. meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters with Mladic and certain things are discussed. This is really the next one in line. And then after that, we had another one that's in evidence that says that at -- I think it's at the meeting of 10.30, certain things occurred. These -- again, this is a major historical document from a person that was in the middle of these events, Mr. Vasic. And as you can tell from the -- from our filings, this is something that -- our version of it was unintelligible, largely. So it took us a while to really get a clear indication that we had this document and what it said. I mean that was -- and that happens with all these documents, and it wasn't until relatively recently that we realised that we did have -- that that wasn't the same as one of the other documents, that it was the new -- the missing link. There was some -- when it was first obtained, I seemed to recall something like it but I wasn't sure if it existed and I kept asking people for it. And we ended up finding this bad translation and we went down and found it recently, as we tried to point out the high points of that in the motion. So that's sort of the little background into this thing. Now, in particular it actually -- my memory of what it says is that it makes a comment about -- General Vasic says -- It speaks of the able-bodied men. I'm not sure I've seen any document that speaks of the able-bodied men of Potocari. These are, as you know, the men that are soon to be killed. So that is the -- something that I would -- I know Your Honours would be very interested in. But now that Ms. Stewart has given me the document, let me go a little bit more routinely through it. Point one in the document -- well, the document first talks about a 10.30 meeting was held, and it identifies some of the people that were there, General Mladic, Vasic, Deronjic, Karremans, and then the Muslims. Interestingly enough, leaving out some of the other army people that we know from other evidence that were there. But then it goes on to list the conclusions of, as you know, important meeting. "According to the Muslims, there are 25.000 people in the base in Potocari." This is, again, as Mr. Stojanovic said, does give us some indication of what, at least the Muslims think, there may be in Potocari, which is something. Then it talks about: "10 per cent are conscripts from 17 to 60 years old." Again, as you recall, at that meeting, the Dutch learned that Mladic wanted the people 17 to 60 screened as war criminals, which was reiterated by Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Deronjic saying that he is the one saying it, the Dutch saying that Mladic said it. In any event, those critical people are discussed. And this actually gives us a potential number, that 10 per cent of 25.000 are able-bodied men. As we look at the evidence that is adduced, we'll determine how reliable that figure is, but at least it's something that you may consider in this -- in what is an important issue. How many men were separated at Potocari? Because obviously that goes to the nature of the -- and the size of the crime that's happening in Bratunac. "They want to leave the camp voluntarily and go to Tuzla or Kladanj and request assistance." Well, I think this goes fundamentally to the forcible transfer, and of course, we don't think this is a credible statement, but certainly it's in an official document that the Court should review. As I hope, and I'm sure the Court is aware of by now, it's been the object of the Prosecution to present relevant and important evidence, no matter what it says, be it intercepts, be it documents, we, of course, think you need the whole picture. This is one of those whole-picture documents that you need to see, to see if you think that is a credible statement. Did the Muslims really want to leave? And the -- perhaps the most interesting statement in this document is at number four: "It was decided to grant their requests and with UNPROFOR assistance, presence, and provision of fuel for transportation, the trucks were provided, boarding of vehicles will commence at 1400 hours, an escort will be provided to Kladanj." Well, that's a nice official start date of what the evidence has suggested but anyway, having an official document, as I know you want to outline the facts, this will assist you, I think. But then, this is what is, I think, very interesting. "After the inspection, depending on Mladic's decision, able-bodied men may be allowed to go in order to have other from the woods surrender, since our command urged them to do so." Well, here is one of the very few references to the able-bodied men that are so critical to understanding this case. As you know, the Prosecution is arguing that the decision to kill these men was made sometime between the night of 11 July and the morning of 12 July, when Mladic announced the separation. And this is fundamental to our case, and I think Mr. Karnavas has made clear that he thinks -- that he will be arguing the -- and I won't argue for Mr. Karnavas, but he will argue that this decision was made at a later time and so this is a key issue. And here we have Mr. Vasic interpreting it. And it -- the Prosecution's interpretation of this is that Mr. Vasic has not been clued in on the plan to murder those men, and Mr. Karnavas will speak for himself and we'll have evidence on that, and he will suggest that I would guess that there is no plan at that point to kill men. It could also mean that Vasic is aware of the plan but is covering himself. So you may hear various interpretations of this. But this is a fundamental and important issue. I'm sure that Mr. Karnavas and I agree that this is a document you should see so that we can argue it properly. And then there's again more information about the various MUP units and where they are, which -- may help you in terms of sorting out some of the MUP evidence that's come in. And that is -- can be important, but for me to explain why that's important would be going beyond the scope of what I should be doing here now. I don't want to argue my case. But I don't think -- I'm almost positive we would all like this document in for basically some of the reasons I've said and I'm sure Mr. Karnavas will agree with me and he will have his own reasons. So I can sit down and let him give his reasons and maybe I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I guess different minds can converge at points in time in this particular trial. I agree with Mr. McCloskey. And when this information was brought to my attention, I had said that I would concur that it should come in, as I had indicated - and Mr. McCloskey's correct - with Mr. Waespi that I did not have any objections. And I want to just clarify that point. Because with the previous documents I had heard a different explanation and given the initial explanation, Mr. McCloskey caused me a little bit of an anxiety attack, hence my recitation. So I just wanted to clear that point with the previous documents, but I don't object to this particular document. And having heard the Court's reasons and having heard the Prosecution's response to my -- reply to my response, I'm comfortable with respect to the previous ruling that the Court made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we had the opportunity to study this document, and the only thing that I would like to say right now regarding our defence, in view of the time and place that this report by Mr. Vasic refers to, and according to our information, the Prosecution received this document from Mr. Vasic, that perhaps this would be a good opportunity, in view of the importance of this document and in view of the quality of the document - and you cannot really see the contents properly from it - that it would be a good opportunity on our part to propose that Mr. Vasic be brought as a witness, as a Prosecution witness, and to testify as to the circumstances the document refers to. And under such conditions, perhaps then we could accept the evidence and the exhibits that the Prosecution is already to an certain extent making use of already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning of the quality of the original document, Mr. McCloskey, do you have anything to say on that aspect? Because it is really a problem because the faintness of the print of that document is -- would you please tell us: How do you or how the interpreters could distinguish words in this kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's my understanding from our study -- recent study that this document was obtained in a search of the -- of Zvornik. And we were provided some documents by Mr. Vasic in various interviews. I don't believe this is one of them. And I was -- I will sort that out. But like a lot of these old documents -- the original is readable. And so what happened was we were able to at least make out a 12 July date in the computer filing and a little bit more information. Then we went down to the vault, we got the original, and the interpreter worked from the original. And we've tried to get a decent photocopy of that original, but -- and we can -- we probably can get a better one if we send it out to the pros that we sometimes use. But we're very confident in the translation because they were able to see the original, and of course, we can bring the original to everyone so they can take a look at it and see it. But we do feel that we have one of these original very -- probably, it may disappear in the next ten years, it's that kind of paper. But it's readable and it's available. Now, regarding -- could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we don't have much time and we will be in court tomorrow, but it has to do with the time as far as -- that will be allocated to the Defence in order to go to the field, make the list, present the list, and so on and so forth. And we've been, I think, magnanimous in allowing the Prosecutor to bring in additional witnesses, and this has caused us some delays. And so I'm going to be asking, just so you know, so you can prepare yourself a little bit for tomorrow, that we resume April 5 -- the Defence case starts on April 5. Because I think Mr. Blagojevic indicated a very valid point with respect to Vasic. I -- but I've also been trying to make a very long list of witnesses, including others that the Prosecution has not brought in. So -- but we need to go back into the field and we need to re-assess and then of course, I wanted to meet with Mr. Blagojevic and give him the list to see if he wished to add anybody to the list. So I don't think physically it's possible for us to get everything ready for us to resume putting on our case before April 5. So that's the target date that I'm asking the Court. So that way when I say it tomorrow, there won't be any surprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if we have time tomorrow. It depends on when we will finish, especially on the Friday afternoon sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that Mr. McCloskey indicated that he was going to take one session. And frankly, from my understanding of the witness, I don't foresee taking more than a session. I mean, I think even less than a session for the cross-examination. So I don't -- I'm positive that we're going to be finishing up early. I just wanted to alert the Court as to the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I think the other day we made a ruling that you might file your 98 bis filings three days after the finish of the Prosecution's case. That is still valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. And I'm not quibbling whether those were business days or whether those included the weekend. I'm not pushing on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a subject we could discuss tomorrow if we have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But it's the other part that I'm really worried about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, just one question to you: I understand that you could make your closing argument after your case is finished or you could make it at the very end of the Defence case. What's your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I think it's time for the break. And we'll resume tomorrow afternoon in Courtroom III at 2.15. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
